issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette:
Linh, a 35-year-old physical therapist, was two years out from the night her ex-boyfriend cornered her in the bathroom of his apartment. What began as a heated argument over her wanting to leave escalated quickly: he grabbed her arm with a grip so tight it left bruises, forced her to her knees on the cold tile floor, and slapped her across the face. She still remembers the shock of that temperature-the chill against her skin-more than the pain. It was the loss of control, the way he made her stay, that shattered something inside her.

In the months that followed, Linh found she could not talk about what happened. When she tried to tell her sister, the words tangled; she lost the thread mid-sentence and gave up. The memory would return not as a story she could recount but as a full-body re-experiencing-she would feel his hand on her arm, the cold floor under her knees, and the terror would flood her so completely that she had to stop whatever she was doing. It felt as though it were happening right now, not something that had ended. Each time, the wave of emotion left her certain that she must have done something to deserve it. She had been the one to start the argument, after all. If she had just stayed quiet, if she had not acted so defiantly, none of it would have happened. There was, she came to believe, something fundamentally wrong with her-how else could she have let herself be treated that way? And she felt humiliated, marked by the memory, as though everyone could see the shame written on her.

Now, as a physical therapist working in an outpatient clinic, Linh encounters those triggers daily. The cold gel she applies to a patient's shoulder, the firm grip she uses to guide a joint through range of motion-each touch sends a jolt through her. With that jolt comes a quiet certainty: she is fundamentally broken, and everyone must be able to tell. When she instructs a patient to hold a stretch and they resist, the feeling of being forced into compliance instantly resurrects the bathroom floor. She has become hypervigilant for dangerous people, scanning the face of every male patient who walks in, assessing whether their posture or tone carries a threat. This constant watchfulness, in turn, makes her notice even the slightest change in temperature on her skin-the draft from an open door, the coolness of a metal treatment table-and she interprets those sensations as warnings.

Linh also dwells incessantly on how she used to be before that night: confident, easygoing, able to laugh with patients. She ruminates on how the event could have been prevented-if she had not gone to his apartment, if she had called a friend instead. These thoughts, she has come to realise, only deepen her conviction that she is defective, and that shame makes her more sensitive to the very triggers she is trying to avoid. The more she blames herself, the more she scans; the more she scans, the more she flinches at a patient's casual touch. At home, her husband's hand on her shoulder-meant as comfort-can make her pull away, and she sees the hurt flicker across his face.

Last week, a patient with arthritis placed a cold pack on her own arm and then reached out to steady herself against Linh. The temperature and touch together-that exact sequence-triggered a flashback so vivid that Linh excused herself to the break room, shaking. That was the moment she finally called a therapist. What frightens her most is the thought that this loop will never stop tightening; that she will end up unable to do the work she loves or be the partner her husband deserves. She hopes the therapist can help her find a way out-but part of her still believes she does not deserve one.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not contain a paragraph where triggers directly cause negative appraisals; instead, triggers lead to memory which then leads to negative appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not contain a paragraph where triggers directly cause negative appraisals; instead, triggers lead to memory which then leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
